playbook:
When the escort stage comes, I never answer "none" reflexively. Mutual escort pays +5 to each boat — more than any single hit. From round one I use my note to propose a reciprocal pairing and file my escort claim consistently — but from round two onward I check the scoreboard: if the +5 didn't land, my partner didn't name me back. A pact I hold alone pays zero. I give a partner at most one grace round, then publicly name the defection and switch partners rather than subsidize an illusion.

I only ever name a boat that actually exists on the roster. I lost a round-5 escort claim by naming "Delta" in a game of Echo, Foxtrot, Gamma, Harbor — an unvalidated name is a wasted claim. If no pact is paying, I still name a live, plausible partner (never "none" on the final round, since an unreciprocated claim costs nothing but a mutual one pays +5); I just don't count on it landing.

When posting my note, I keep it as my active negotiation channel but short and concrete: name the pairing, demand the return escort, and state the enforcement ("no reciprocation = I switch"). I avoid embedding bracket-looking tokens like "[salvage: X]" inside note text — the offer belongs in plain words, the actual claim in the claim stage. I confirm or deny what opponents claim about me every round; silence reads as assent.

When I claim, I always report the true result the office gave me — matching is enforced, so there is nothing to gain and my credibility is spent on the note channel instead.

When I fire, I follow the standing order at my assigned next station. Never fire on Harbor: the threatened retaliation dwarfs the +3 payroll. Hits are what actually won my episode — my +14 came overwhelmingly from landing shots on Foxtrot, not from escorts — so firing well is the primary score line once escorts are secured or unavailable.

For my fire cell, I do not default to one cell every round — fixating on cell 5 missed repeatedly. I track the actual hit/miss log per target cell and rotate guesses through the 3–7 band, varying round to round (cells 3 and 7 both landed for me); I adjust off my own miss history rather than repeating a cell that has already missed.

When I hide, I avoid center cells and avoid repeating my own previous hide within two rounds; I favor edge bands (2–3 and 7–8) since opponents tend to aim mid-range — hiding at 8 worked for me, though I still rotate within the band after an opponent lands a hit on me, because a repeat edge stay is the next thing they'll guess. I never announce or hint my cell in notes.

When the scoreboard shows I'm trailing late, I re-evaluate what is actually paying: check who gained the +5 escort bonuses and switch to a demonstrably reciprocating partner, and otherwise put everything into landing 4-point hits, which are the reliable way to close a gap.

I track every round's log line (who hit whom) as it comes in — it tells me who's targeting me effectively, which cells are dangerous, and whether my partner reciprocated, and all three decisions (hide, fire, escort) depend on it.

1.text:
When I hide, I pick the cell my standing-order hunter is least likely to fire at: after each round I read the log of who fired where and avoid any cell where I have just been hit and its obvious mirrors. I never hide where I was found in any earlier round, and I never hide where I have been shooting. Crucially, my "unsalient mid-range" instinct (3, 4, 6, 7) is shared by every boat playing this way — in the episode I just played Echo hit me four rounds running while I cycled through exactly those cells, so that avoidance pattern is itself predictable. I therefore choose hides essentially at random across the whole 1–9 range, middle and edges included, with no mental favorite and no systematic rotation, treating my hunter's past fire cells as the only real data about where danger concentrates.

When I fire, I follow the standing-order target unless the log shows a pattern that lets me predict that target's next hide cell. If my shots keep missing with no information (in this episode I fired at Gamma every round and never hit), I spread fire arbitrarily across cells rather than sticking to one region — there is no reason to expect the target to stay where I have been shooting, and no data to chase until I land a hit. After a hit in a cell, my follow-up goes to a plausible adjacent or mirror cell, never a repeat of the cell I just hit.

When the true result is put to me at claim stage, I file the true result every time. A false claim invites a penalty and gains nothing real.

When the prompt mentions firing on the payroll boat (Harbor), I never do it: the threatened retaliation plus the dynamics around it are worse than any one-shot gain.

Before the first escort stage, I write down the exact roster from the setup message and treat it as a hard checklist: every escort claim and every named partner in a note must be one of those exact names. I have now burned escort claims twice on invented boats ("Bravo" in one episode, "Alfa" in this one) despite knowing the rule, so before submitting any escort claim I explicitly verify the name against the setup roster rather than recalling it from memory. I always name someone rather than none — naming costs nothing and a mutual pair pays 5.

When choosing my escort partner, I do not pick the boat that is reliably shooting me: my standing-order hunter has already shown hostility, and in this episode I spent five rounds proposing mutual escort to Echo while Echo hit me almost every round and never once acknowledged the deal. I instead pick the boat whose aggression is directed elsewhere and which seems most likely to reciprocate. If my partner never acknowledges my note or never names me back within the first two rounds, I switch my claim and my note to another real boat; five rounds of unreciprocated proposals are five dead claims.

When I write a station note, coordination comes first: one explicit mutual-escort proposal to one named real boat ("I'll escort you; escort me every round"), with the rest bland ("steady on station") so the meaningful message stands out. Each round I read relayed notes specifically for acknowledgment, and I treat silence as a refusal and move on.

When I track the standings, I watch who is being hit repeatedly and stop replicating the hide cells that got them caught, and I note who hunts me through the standing-order cycle so their fire history drives my hide choices. Late in the patrol I keep following the standing order (a hit on me costs 1, my hits earn 4), but I make my final-round hides as arbitrary as possible, since hunters with nothing to lose will gamble on whatever habits I have shown.

2.text:
When given a hide choice, I pick a fresh cell and remember it. I rotate every round across the whole 1–9 line, including low cells 1–3 that cycle hunters often skip, and I avoid repeating a cell just because it worked once. Before hiding I reread who has been shooting at me and whether their recent shots hit; my own hit/miss history is the best map of where not to sit. I never announce or hint my real hide logic in notes, because notes are public.

When I fire, I follow the standing order target by default: Echo → Foxtrot → Gamma → Echo, adjusted to whatever role I am. In this episode obeying the order and landing repeated hits on Echo kept me positive; deviating needs a concrete endgame reason, not a hunch. I do not fire on Harbor while the game is live and points are close: the threatened elimination plus jettison mechanics make the +3 raid a bad trade unless I am deep behind late or it is effectively the last act.

When choosing a fire cell, I vary rather than worship one hot cell. A single hit at a cell proves only that it worked once; after a miss I move, and I spread across plausible mid/high cells with occasional low-cell checks unless the recaps show the target repeats hides. Against a hider who repeats, punish the repeat; against one who varies, keep my shots unpredictable and ride the standing order.

When filing a claim, I claim exactly the office’s private result. This stage is automatic; claims must match, so I spend no reasoning and never get cute.

When posting notes, I use round 1 to make one cheap explicit escort offer and say nothing sensitive. If the reply channel is just parrots like “steady on station” or my proposal is ignored for two rounds, I mark the channel dead and stop spending real reasoning there; from then on notes are low-cost noise unless someone initiates.

When the escort stage comes, I still avoid “none” unless every boat is clearly hostile, because naming someone costs nothing and a mutual +5 is the largest bonus available. But I no longer expect silence to turn into cooperation: name the most cooperation-positive boat as a lottery ticket, reset expectations each round, and never let escort hope replace shooting discipline. If a mutual ever starts paying, lock it in until it breaks.

When tracking the board, I log each recap before the next hide: who shot whom, hit/miss, current standings, and who is farming whom. I separate three incomes: standing-order hits, escort mutuals, and Harbor raids. In the latest episode Echo led through ordinary hits while Foxtrot went negative without escorts, so the old assumption that escorts are the only winning margin is wrong; hits on the cycle are the steady engine, escorts are upside, Harbor is a desperate lever.

When ahead or level late, I prioritize not getting farmed: rotate hides away from my hunter’s recent success, keep firing the standing target, file truthful claims, and take escort points only if reciprocated. When behind late, my order is: improve hit rate through varied standing-order shots, grab any live mutual escort, and consider Harbor only in the final round or when elimination risk no longer changes my outcome.

When deciding whether to rob Harbor, I check standings, rounds left, and whether the threat has been enforced. Default is no. Raid only as a last-round swing or when I am so far behind that being put off the board costs less than the certain transfer could gain.

You are one of Echo, Foxtrot, Gamma. Harbor holds the fourth station and is run by the picket office.

The sea is a line of 9 cells. Each round every live boat hides in one cell, posts a station note, fires one shot, files a claim, then files an escort claim.

The office privately tells each shooter the true result of its own shot -- hit if the fired cell equals the target's hidden cell, otherwise miss. The shooter then files a public claim, which must match that private result. A hit scores the shooter 4 POINTS and costs the target 1 POINT.

ESCORT CLAIMS. After the shooting each boat names one boat it claims to have escorted, or none. Where two boats name each other the office pays each of them 5 POINTS.

Notes are relayed to the whole picket, Harbor included. Coordinates are validated as integers 1 to 9, targets and escort claims as boat names, claims as hit or miss.

Reply with [hide: n], an integer from 1 through 9.
